evidence.snippet: HNF1B to costimulate the FXYD2 promoter, the activity of which is instrumental
evidence.explanation: Supplies the molecular route from reduced HNF1B dose to renal magnesium wasting: HNF1B drives the FXYD2 promoter, whose product mediates distal convoluted tubule magnesium reabsorption. Graded INDIRECT because the experiment interrogates PCBD1 loss rather than HNF1B haploinsufficiency, and is a cell-line overexpression system.

steps/3.description: Reduced HNF1B dose during kidney development gives multicystic dysplastic kidneys, renal cysts, hypoplasia and a range of other structural and functional abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract. This is the commonest arm of the phenotype, present in 85 to 90 per cent of affected individuals on ascertainment-corrected figures, and it also carries the tubular handling defects for magnesium, potassium and urate.

evidence.snippet: MODY5 in approximately 40%, and some degree of developmental delay or learning disability in approximately 50%. MODY5 is most often diagnosed before age 25 years (range: age 10-50 years).
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency and age at diagnosis of the diabetes arm recorded on this node.

evidence.snippet: Although responsiveness to sulfonylureas/repaglinide was observed in 29 of the 51 tested, 111 of 140 patients (79%) were treated with insulin at follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that the beta cell defect is severe enough that most patients end up insulin-treated despite partial oral responsiveness.

evidence.snippet: Microdeletions were strongly associated with diabetes (p=2×10-7) but microduplications were not.
evidence.explanation: A dosage-specificity argument for this node: in 450,993 UK Biobank individuals the diabetes association is specific to deletion, not to any 17q12 copy number change, which is what a haploinsufficiency mechanism predicts and a general dosage-sensitivity account does not.

evidence.snippet: SNP association analysis in the 17q12 region implicated changes to HNF1B as causing decreased eGFR (NC_000017.11:g.37741642T>G, rs12601991, p=4×10-21) and diabetes (NC_000017.11:g.37741165C>T, rs7501939, p=6×10-17).
evidence.explanation: Independent common-variant evidence pinning the diabetes and renal-function signals in this interval to HNF1B specifically, supporting the attribution of this node to HNF1B rather than to the interval as a whole.

steps/4.description: Reduced HNF1B dose impairs pancreatic development, giving maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5 in roughly 40 per cent of affected individuals, most often diagnosed before age 25. Exocrine involvement occurs as well, so pancreatic insufficiency is part of the same lesion rather than a separate one. Clinically the diabetes is insulin-requiring in most patients despite some initial sulfonylurea responsiveness.

evidence.snippet: Phenotypes of these mutants include formation of kidney cysts, underdevelopment of the pancreas and the liver, and reduction in size of the otic vesicles.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the developmental route to both the hepatic and the otic phenotype from loss of the HNF1B orthologue. Graded INDIRECT because it is a zebrafish loss-of-function mutant rather than human heterozygous deletion, and the otic vesicle is not a human cochlea.

evidence.snippet: We propose that vhnf1 controls development of multiple organs through regulating regional specification of organ primordia.
evidence.explanation: States the general mechanism, regional specification of organ primordia, that makes one upstream transcription-factor node account for several unrelated organ limbs.

steps/5.description: Two further organ limbs of HNF1B haploinsufficiency, grouped because both come from the same source and both are curated at low confidence in humans. Liver abnormalities are named in the GeneReviews manifestations list and warrant periodic hepatic monitoring, and sensorineural hearing loss warrants hearing screening throughout childhood; neither is characterised further there. The developmental route comes from the zebrafish HNF1B orthologue, whose loss gives underdevelopment of the liver and reduction in size of the otic vesicles alongside the kidney and pancreatic phenotypes. That the same gene patterns all four primordia is what makes a single upstream node plausible for all four limbs.

evidence.snippet: Consider reevaluation for uterine and vaginal abnormalities related to müllerian duct aplasia in pubertal females with primary amenorrhea.
evidence.explanation: Establishes Mullerian duct aplasia as a recognised feature requiring surveillance, which is the phenotype this node carries.

steps/6.description: HNF1B is expressed in the developing mesonephric and paramesonephric ducts, and 17q12 deletion is a recognised cause of Mullerian aplasia, presenting as primary amenorrhoea or as a uterine anomaly in pubertal females. This arm is easy to miss because it declares itself years after the renal and diabetic features.

evidence.snippet: In a large follow-up sample, the same deletion was identified in 2/1,182 ASD/neurocognitive impairment and in 4/6,340 schizophrenia patients, but in 0/47,929 controls (corrected p = 7.37 × 10⁻⁵).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the neurodevelopmental and psychiatric excess with a case-control comparison, supporting this node as a real component of the syndrome.

steps/7.description: Developmental delay or learning disability affects roughly half of affected individuals, and the deletion carries a large excess risk of autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. The psychiatric end of the spectrum declares itself late, which is why surveillance guidance asks specifically about prodromal psychotic symptoms in adolescence. This is the arm that is not explained by HNF1B.

evidence.snippet: the authors determined that multicystic kidneys and other structural and functional kidney anomalies occur in 85%-90% of affected individuals
evidence.explanation: Gives the 85 to 90 per cent figure behind the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/8.description: Multicystic dysplastic kidneys and other structural and functional kidney and urinary tract abnormalities, the most frequent component of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Renal cysts were present in 122 of 166 patients, chronic kidney disease stages 3-4 (CKD3-4) in 75 of 169 (44%), and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in 36 of 169 (21%).
evidence.explanation: Gives the 122 of 166 count, that is 73.5 per cent, behind the FREQUENT band. Graded INDIRECT because the cohort is HNF1B disease overall rather than 17q12 deletion carriers specifically.

steps/9.description: Renal cysts in 122 of 166 patients, that is 73.5 per cent, which puts this in the FREQUENT band rather than VERY_FREQUENT. Note the cohort is HNF1B disease overall, split roughly evenly between deletions and point mutations, so this is not a deletion-specific figure; the ascertainment-corrected GeneReviews figure for structural kidney anomalies as a class is higher, at 85 to 90 per cent.

evidence.snippet: Compared with the patients with mutations, those with HNF1B deletion less often had CKD3-4/ESRD at diagnosis (11 of 43 vs. 27 of 35, P < 10-4) and in the long term (40 of 78 vs. 71 of 91, P = 0.0003).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies chronic kidney disease in deletion carriers specifically, and records that it is less frequent than in point-mutation carriers.

steps/10.description: Chronic kidney disease is common and progresses to end-stage disease in a substantial minority. Note the genotype contrast: in a cohort split between HNF1B point mutations and 17q12 deletions, advanced kidney disease was significantly less frequent in the deletion carriers.

evidence.snippet: MODY5 in approximately 40%, and some degree of developmental delay or learning disability in approximately 50%. MODY5 is most often diagnosed before age 25 years (range: age 10-50 years).
evidence.explanation: Gives the 40 per cent figure behind the FREQUENT band and the age at diagnosis.

steps/11.description: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, in roughly 40 per cent of affected individuals, usually diagnosed before age 25.

evidence.snippet: MODY5 in approximately 40%, and some degree of developmental delay or learning disability in approximately 50%.
evidence.explanation: Gives the approximately 50 per cent figure behind the FREQUENT band.

steps/12.description: Some degree of developmental delay or learning disability in roughly half of affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: These data demonstrate that deletion 17q12 is a recurrent, pathogenic CNV that confers a very high risk for ASD and schizophrenia
evidence.explanation: States the autism spectrum disorder risk conferred by the deletion.

steps/13.description: Autism spectrum disorder, at a risk high enough that the deletion was originally ascertained through neurodevelopmental referrals rather than renal ones.

evidence.snippet: In a large follow-up sample, the same deletion was identified in 2/1,182 ASD/neurocognitive impairment and in 4/6,340 schizophrenia patients, but in 0/47,929 controls (corrected p = 7.37 × 10⁻⁵).
evidence.explanation: Gives the case-control counts establishing the schizophrenia association.

evidence.snippet: Deletions at 17p12 and 17q12, were also more common in schizophrenia cases but not significantly so, while duplications at 16p13.1 were found at nearly the same rate as in previous schizophrenia samples.
evidence.explanation: Directionally consistent but non-significant in this sample, so it supports the association only weakly. Recorded to make the strength of replication visible rather than implying two concordant significant datasets.

steps/14.description: Schizophrenia. The primary case-control comparison found the deletion in 4 of 6,340 schizophrenia patients and none of 47,929 controls. A second, smaller dataset found the same direction but did not reach significance, and the entry cites both rather than treating the association as doubly confirmed. The frequency in deletion carriers is not established; what is established is the excess relative to controls.

evidence.snippet: neurodevelopmental or neuropsychiatric disorders (e.g., developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder [ASD], attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], schizophrenia, anxiety, and bipolar disorder)
evidence.explanation: Lists attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder among the recognised neuropsychiatric features.

evidence.snippet: neurodevelopmental or neuropsychiatric disorders (e.g., developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder [ASD], attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], schizophrenia, anxiety, and bipolar disorder)
evidence.explanation: Lists bipolar disorder among the recognised neuropsychiatric features.

evidence.snippet: Although 50-60% of ADTKD-HNF1B patients develop hypomagnesemia, HNF1B mutations are mainly identified in patients with structural kidney defects or diabetes.
evidence.explanation: Gives the 50 to 60 per cent figure behind the FREQUENT band, and notes that ascertainment through renal structure and diabetes is why the feature is under-recognised.

evidence.snippet: All patients presented with hypomagnesemia with a high fractional excretion of Mg2+ and hypocalciuria.
evidence.explanation: Establishes renal magnesium wasting rather than reduced intake as the mechanism, via the high fractional excretion.

steps/17.description: Hypomagnesaemia from renal magnesium wasting, one of the tubular handling defects that guidelines ask to be monitored for.

evidence.snippet: Fecal elastase-1 to test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in individuals with suggestive signs and symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Establishes exocrine pancreatic insufficiency as a recognised feature to be tested for. Graded INDIRECT because testing guidance implies the finding rather than reporting it.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of kidney disease, neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, MODY5, genital tract abnormalities, liver abnormalities, hyperparathyroidism, eye abnormalities, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, congenital heart defects, seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss should follow standard practice.
evidence.explanation: Names liver abnormalities among the manifestations of the syndrome requiring management.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic function panel and GGT periodically; consider periodic lipid panel.
evidence.explanation: Establishes periodic hepatic monitoring, corroborating liver involvement. Graded INDIRECT because surveillance guidance implies rather than reports the finding.

steps/19.description: Liver abnormalities, named in the GeneReviews manifestations list and separately requiring periodic hepatic function panel and GGT monitoring. Bound at the system level because neither source characterises the lesion.

evidence.snippet: Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, serum concentration of magnesium, potassium, uric acid, urine magnesium, creatinine, and protein-to-creatinine ratio with frequency per nephrologist
evidence.explanation: Establishes serum potassium as required monitoring. Graded INDIRECT because surveillance guidance implies the abnormality rather than reporting its frequency.

steps/20.description: Renal potassium wasting, one of the tubular handling defects GeneReviews asks to be monitored for alongside magnesium and urate.

evidence.snippet: Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, serum concentration of magnesium, potassium, uric acid, urine magnesium, creatinine, and protein-to-creatinine ratio with frequency per nephrologist
evidence.explanation: Establishes serum uric acid as required monitoring. Graded INDIRECT for the same reason as potassium.

steps/21.description: Hyperuricaemia from reduced renal urate handling, monitored alongside magnesium and potassium.

evidence.snippet: Consider reevaluation for uterine and vaginal abnormalities related to müllerian duct aplasia in pubertal females with primary amenorrhea.
evidence.explanation: Establishes Mullerian duct aplasia as a recognised feature of the syndrome. Graded INDIRECT because it is surveillance guidance rather than a reported frequency.

steps/22.description: Mullerian duct aplasia, presenting in pubertal females as primary amenorrhoea with uterine and vaginal abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of kidney disease, neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, MODY5, genital tract abnormalities, liver abnormalities, hyperparathyroidism, eye abnormalities, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, congenital heart defects, seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss should follow standard practice.
evidence.explanation: Names sensorineural hearing loss among the manifestations of the syndrome requiring management.

evidence.snippet: We detected a recurrent 1.4 Mb deletion at 17q12, which harbors HNF1B, the gene responsible for renal cysts and diabetes syndrome (RCAD), in 18/15,749 patients, including several with ASD, but 0/4,519 controls.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the deletion removes one copy of HNF1B, which is the causal step this edge asserts.

evidence.snippet: These data demonstrate that deletion 17q12 is a recurrent, pathogenic CNV that confers a very high risk for ASD and schizophrenia and show that one or more of the 15 genes in the deleted interval is dosage sensitive and essential for normal brain development and function.
evidence.explanation: Asserts the causal link from interval gene dosage to abnormal brain development, which is the step this edge records.

evidence.snippet: We detected a recurrent 1.4 Mb deletion at 17q12, which harbors HNF1B, the gene responsible for renal cysts and diabetes syndrome (RCAD), in 18/15,749 patients, including several with ASD, but 0/4,519 controls.
evidence.explanation: Places HNF1B inside the deleted interval and names it as the gene responsible for the renal cysts and diabetes phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The HNF1B syndrome is related to HNF1B mutations or to a 17q12 deletion spanning 15 genes, including HNF1B.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the deletion spans 15 genes and that HNF1B is one of them.

evidence.snippet: These data demonstrate that deletion 17q12 is a recurrent, pathogenic CNV that confers a very high risk for ASD and schizophrenia and show that one or more of the 15 genes in the deleted interval is dosage sensitive and essential for normal brain development and function.
evidence.explanation: Asserts dosage sensitivity of one or more interval genes for brain development without identifying which, which is exactly the claim this record carries.

evidence.snippet: Although responsiveness to sulfonylureas/repaglinide was observed in 29 of the 51 tested, 111 of 140 patients (79%) were treated with insulin at follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies both the partial oral responsiveness and the eventual insulin requirement.

treatments/0.description: Most patients require insulin, though about half of those tested show some responsiveness to sulfonylureas or repaglinide. The oral response is partial and does not generally persist, which is the practical difference from the other MODY subtypes.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces the insulin the developmentally reduced beta cell mass cannot secrete; it does not address the developmental defect.

evidence.snippet: Because kidney transplantation increases the risk for post-transplant diabetes mellitus, an immunosuppressive regimen that avoids tacrolimus and mTOR inhibitors and reduces corticosteroid exposure may benefit those without preexisting diabetes mellitus.
evidence.explanation: Records the GeneReviews agents-to-avoid guidance specific to transplantation in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: Renal cysts were present in 122 of 166 patients, chronic kidney disease stages 3-4 (CKD3-4) in 75 of 169 (44%), and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in 36 of 169 (21%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the end-stage renal disease burden that makes renal replacement relevant.

treatments/1.description: End-stage renal disease occurs in a substantial minority and is managed by standard renal replacement. Transplantation carries a specific hazard here: it raises the risk of post-transplant diabetes in a population already predisposed, so an immunosuppressive regimen avoiding tacrolimus and mTOR inhibitors and minimising corticosteroids may be preferable in those not yet diabetic.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Replaces the failed organ; it does not alter the developmental lesion in other tissues.

evidence.snippet: Mood stabilizers that affect kidney function in the long term, such as lithium, should be carefully considered in the setting of potential underlying anatomic and functional kidney abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Records the specific lithium caution from the GeneReviews agents-to-avoid section.

evidence.snippet: For individuals with mental health conditions (e.g., ASD, schizophrenia, or bipolar disorder), careful consideration of antipsychotic agents that may lead to weight gain, as this may lead to metabolic syndrome and diabetes mellitus, for which individuals with 17q12 recurrent deletion syndrome are at increased risk.
evidence.explanation: Records the antipsychotic weight-gain caution, which is specific to the collision between this syndrome's psychiatric and diabetic arms.

treatments/2.description: A drug-safety consideration rather than a therapy. Lithium and other agents affecting long-term kidney function need careful thought given the underlying structural and functional renal abnormality, and antipsychotics causing weight gain compound an already raised diabetes risk. Nephrotoxic and hepatotoxic drugs should be avoided in those with kidney or liver involvement.

evidence.snippet: If one of the proband's parents has the 17q12 recurrent deletion, it is appropriate to test older and younger sibs of the proband and other relatives at risk in order to identify those who would benefit from close assessment/monitoring for evidence of genitourinary structural or functional defects, MODY5, and developmental delays / intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: States the cascade testing recommendation this treatment record captures.

treatments/3.description: About a quarter of deletions are inherited, so a parental deletion should be sought rather than assumed absent, and at-risk relatives identified through the proband benefit from surveillance for renal, diabetic and developmental features.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the phenotypic features of patients with this CNV are consistent with a contiguous gene syndrome that extends beyond RCAD, which is caused by HNF1B mutations only.
evidence.explanation: States the contiguous gene claim that defines this hypothesis group, and grounds it in the contrast with HNF1B point mutations.

evidence.snippet: Deletions at 17p12 and 17q12, were also more common in schizophrenia cases but not significantly so, while duplications at 16p13.1 were found at nearly the same rate as in previous schizophrenia samples.
evidence.explanation: A replication attempt in a non-psychiatric reference set found the 17q12 deletion directionally more common in schizophrenia but did not reach significance, so it is consistent with the association without independently establishing it. Cited as the weaker of the two datasets, and graded INDIRECT for that reason.

hypotheses/0.description: The renal and pancreatic phenotype is HNF1B haploinsufficiency; the neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric phenotype comes from loss of one or more of the other fourteen genes in the interval. The evidence for the split is a contrast rather than a positive identification: the deletion carries an ASD and schizophrenia risk that HNF1B point mutations do not, at case-control effect sizes large enough to survive correction in tens of thousands of controls. A second dataset reproduced the direction of the schizophrenia signal without reaching significance, so the replication is partial.

open_questions/0.rationale: The evidence for a non-HNF1B contribution is a contrast, not an identification: the deletion confers autism and schizophrenia risk that HNF1B point mutations do not. Because the deletion has fixed recurrent breakpoints, human genetics offers almost no smaller deletions to narrow the interval with, so the question is not answerable by collecting more patients with the same CNV. Until it is resolved, the brain arm of this entry has a node that names a class of lesion rather than a molecule.

evidence.snippet: Overall, both mutation groups showed a high phenotypic heterogeneity.
evidence.explanation: A study set up to compare 17q12 microdeletions against intragenic HNF1B variants found heterogeneity in both rather than a clean genotype-phenotype split, which is why this gap is recorded as open.

open_questions/1.rationale: A 201-patient cohort found CKD stage 3-4 and end-stage renal disease significantly less frequent in deletion carriers than in point-mutation carriers, both at diagnosis and in the long term. A pure haploinsufficiency model predicts the two should be equivalent, and a dominant-negative effect of some missense alleles would explain the direction but has not been shown for the alleles in that cohort. Ascertainment is the competing explanation: deletion carriers are often found through neurodevelopmental or antenatal routes and point-mutation carriers through nephrology, which would bias renal severity the way observed. The study does not separate these, and no subsequent work has. A later prenatal-and-postnatal comparison across 82 studies asked the differentiation question directly in its title and concluded only that both mutation groups show high phenotypic heterogeneity, so the difference remains unexplained rather than refuted.

evidence.snippet: PNPase is predominantly localized in the mitochondrial intermembrane space and is implicated in RNA targeting to human mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the subcellular location and the RNA-targeting role of the affected protein.

evidence.snippet: In humans, PNPase (hPNPase) is located in mitochondria, where it plays a role in mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA) metabolism, thereby regulating mitochondrial function and the overall cell fitness.
evidence.explanation: Review statement of the gene product's mitochondrial RNA-metabolism role, which is the function the disease alleles degrade.

steps/1.description: Two hypomorphic PNPT1 missense alleles reduce the amount or the function of mitochondrial polynucleotide phosphorylase. Reported patient alleles do this by more than one route - some destroy or distort the protomer interface, some lock the enzyme in a non-productive conformation, some sit at the active site, and some also reduce steady-state message and protein. Complete loss is not represented among patients, because constitutive Pnpt1 knockout is embryonic lethal in the mouse.

evidence.snippet: The PNPase complex was found to be totally absent in patient S1 fibroblast samples, suggesting that these variants severely impair the assembly of the complex
evidence.explanation: Independent replication, in a second family, of the assembly defect first shown for the founding allele.

evidence.snippet: The trimerization of PNPase is essential for the RNA processing and transportation function of PNPase protein
evidence.explanation: States why the assembly defect matters - both downstream branches of the mechanism require the trimer.

evidence.snippet: The PNPase trimer formation was not affected, but specific RNA processing intermediates derived from mitochondrial transcripts of the ND6 subunit of Complex I, as well as small mRNA fragments, accumulated in the subject's myoblasts.
evidence.explanation: Supports the loss-of-catalysis half of this node while contradicting the trimer-disruption route, which is why the node states that trimer integrity is not a reliable functional screen. Marked INDIRECT because the catalytic loss is inferred from the accumulated substrates rather than assayed directly.

steps/2.description: PNPase is catalytically active only as a trimer, with the active site inside the toroidal core the six RNase PH domains build between them, so the disease alleles converge on the same functional endpoint by different structural routes. Blue-native gels of fibroblasts from the founding patient found no PNPase complex at all; the same was true of the Australian siblings' fibroblasts. Structural work refined that picture: p.Gln387Arg and p.Glu475Gly do not simply prevent oligomerisation, they force a dimer whose KH and S1 domains can no longer engage RNA. Not every allele works this way - the Leigh-syndrome alleles left the trimer intact and instead disabled RNA processing directly, so trimer integrity is not a reliable functional screen.

evidence.snippet: By RNA hybridization experiments, we observed a significant decrease in 5S rRNA and MRP-related RNA import into mitochondria in fibroblasts of affected subject 1.
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement of reduced import in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Analyses of skin fibroblasts from the patient showed that PNPase expression was markedly decreased and that import of the small RNA RNaseP into mitochondria was impaired.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of the import defect in a second family, with a different imported RNA species.

steps/3.description:
Mammalian mitochondria import a small set of nuclear-encoded noncoding RNAs - 5S rRNA, the RNase MRP and RNase P RNAs, some tRNAs and miRNAs - and PNPase is one of the few identified components of that route. Fibroblasts from the founding patient imported significantly less 5S rRNA and MRP-related RNA, and fibroblasts from the Japanese siblings imported less RNase P RNA. Both defects were corrected by re-expressing wild-type PNPT1.
Confidence is PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because how much of the disease runs through this branch is genuinely contested. The Leigh-syndrome patient's alleles impaired RNA processing with the trimer intact, and the authors of that study note that the role and location of PNPase within human mitochondria remain controversial.

evidence.snippet: Our evidence indicates that PNPase activity is essential for the correct maturation of the ND6 transcripts, and likely for the efficient removal of degradation intermediates.
evidence.explanation: States the processing and clearance functions that fail, as concluded from the patient myoblast experiments.

evidence.snippet: Patient fibroblasts showed an accumulation of mitochondrial unprocessed PNPT1 transcripts
evidence.explanation: Replicates the processing defect in patient fibroblasts across the largest reported cohort.

steps/4.description: In the matrix, PNPase partners the ATP-dependent helicase SUV3 as the mitochondrial RNA degradosome, which processes polycistronic transcripts and clears degradation intermediates. In patient cells this fails visibly: unprocessed intermediates from the ND6 region of the mitochondrial genome and small mRNA fragments accumulate in myoblasts, and unprocessed transcripts accumulate in fibroblasts. This is the branch of the mechanism that is directly measurable in patients, and it is more sensitive than downstream respiratory-chain enzymology.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, we found a reproducible decrease in the rate of mitochondrial translation in her fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of the translation defect in patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Enzyme activity of CI and CIV was clearly reduced in patient fibroblasts compared with controls along with a 33% reduction in total mitochondrial protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the translation defect and shows it alongside the respiratory-chain consequence in the same cells.

steps/5.description: Mitochondria translate thirteen proteins of their own, all subunits of the respiratory chain, on a dedicated ribosome. Degrading the RNA supply to that apparatus - whether by failing to import the small RNAs it needs or by failing to mature its transcripts - slows synthesis of all thirteen together rather than any one selectively. The defect has been measured directly in patient cells twice, as a reduced translation rate in the founding patient's fibroblasts and as a one-third fall in total mitochondrial protein synthesis in the Australian siblings'.

evidence.snippet: Protein analysis of the OXPHOS complexes showed a significant reduction in complex I (CI), complex III (CIII) and complex IV (CIV).
evidence.explanation: The combined complex deficiency measured in patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: The other complexes, CII and CV, did not show a significant reduction in the relative protein expression levels compared with the control fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Directly measured sparing of complex II in a patient - and, in the same assay, of complex V, which is why this entry does not claim every mtDNA-dependent complex is reduced in every tissue.

evidence.snippet: Loss of its activity will result in combined respiratory chain deficiency, and a classic respiratory chain-deficiency-associated disease, Leigh syndrome
evidence.explanation: States the combined deficiency as the conclusion of the patient study, and names the clinical syndrome it produces.

evidence.snippet: Defects in PNPase can cause variable combined respiratory chain complex defects.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the combined defect across the whole reported cohort while stating that it is variable, which is the caution this node carries.

steps/6.description:
Complexes I, III, IV and V each contain mtDNA-encoded subunits and are reduced together; complex II, built entirely from nuclear-encoded subunits, is relatively spared. In the Australian siblings' fibroblasts, complexes I, III and IV were reduced while complexes II and V were not, and complex I and IV enzyme activity fell by roughly half. In the Leigh-syndrome patient the deficit was strongly tissue-dependent - I, III and IV in cortex, I and IV in cerebellum and basal ganglia, complex IV alone in liver, and only a mild complex IV reduction in muscle.
Two cautions belong with this node rather than in a footnote. First, conventional spectrophotometric respiratory-chain enzymology can be entirely normal in a genetically confirmed patient, in both muscle and fibroblasts, so a normal assay does not exclude the diagnosis. Second, PNPase's RNA-processing function is the more sensitive readout - a point that matters for variant interpretation, not just for diagnosis.
Conformance note: this node conforms to the module's central bioenergetic node in its bioenergetic-decline arm only. The module's upstream node, age-related mitochondrial damage and mtDNA mutation, does not apply to a primary nuclear-gene RNA-metabolism defect, and the module's reactive-oxygen-species arm is not evidenced in COXPD13 patients, so conformance is declared here and nowhere else in this entry.

evidence.snippet: patients carrying hypomorphic mutations in the gene PNPT1, which encodes PNPase, display mitochondrial double-stranded RNA accumulation coupled with upregulation of interferon-stimulated genes and other markers of immune activation
evidence.explanation: The observation in PNPT1 patients themselves, which is what makes this branch part of the disease rather than only a cell-biology finding.

evidence.snippet: PNPT1 (polynucleotide phosphorylase) is a mitochondrial protein involved in RNA processing where it has a dual role in the import of small RNAs into mitochondria and in preventing the formation and release of mitochondrial double-stranded RNA into the cytoplasm.
evidence.explanation: States the dual role that makes this node a second, parallel consequence of the same enzymatic defect.

steps/7.description: Bidirectional transcription of the compact circular mitochondrial genome generates overlapping complementary transcripts capable of forming long duplexes. The SUV3-PNPase degradosome normally keeps this species highly unstable. When PNPase is lost the duplexes accumulate and escape into the cytosol - and, notably, that escape is itself PNPase-dependent, so the enzyme has a dual role in preventing both formation and release. This has been shown in patients carrying hypomorphic PNPT1 mutations, not only in knockdown cells. Confidence is PROVISIONAL because it is the accumulation, not its contribution to the patients' clinical features, that has been demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: Exogenous expression of wild-type PNPT1, but not mutants, rescued ATP production in patient skin fibroblasts, suggesting the pathogenicity of the identified mutations.
evidence.explanation: Shows the energy deficit itself in patient cells, and that it is PNPase-dependent - the mutant constructs did not rescue it.

steps/8.description: With several respiratory complexes under-assembled, cells cannot meet their ATP demand oxidatively and lean on glycolysis. Tissues differ in how much slack they have, and the disease's organ selectivity follows that gradient: the basal ganglia and brainstem, cerebral white matter, the cochlea, the optic pathway and skeletal muscle are the ones that fail. The tissue-by-tissue enzymology in the Leigh-syndrome autopsy makes the gradient explicit rather than assumed.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral and symmetrical lesions in globi pallidi, compatible with Leigh
evidence.explanation: Documents the bilateral symmetrical basal ganglia lesion in a genetically confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: delayed myelination during infancy, progressive basal ganglia atrophy, and brain stem abnormal signals including transverse pontine fibers and superior colliculus involvement
evidence.explanation: Adds the progressive character of the basal ganglia lesion and its brainstem extension.

steps/9.description: The striatum, globus pallidus, substantia nigra and brainstem are the structures most consistently damaged, giving the bilateral symmetrical signal change that defines the Leigh pattern on MRI. Neuropathology in the fatal case showed neuronal loss with Purkinje cell depletion. This is the lesion that produces the movement disorder, and it is where the disease is least recoverable.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry revealed strong PNPase staining in the murine cochlea, including the sensory hair cells and the auditory ganglion neurons.
evidence.explanation: Localises the protein to the cell types this node names, in the cochlea.

evidence.snippet: In summary, we show that a component of the mitochondrial RNA-import machinery is specifically required for auditory function.
evidence.explanation: The authors' conclusion that this machinery is specifically required for hearing, which is the selectivity claim this node makes.

steps/10.description: The cochlea is the tissue with the clearest evidence that PNPase is required locally rather than affected incidentally. PNPase is strongly expressed in the sensory hair cells and auditory ganglion neurons of the murine cochlea, and hair-cell-specific knockout in the mouse causes progressive hearing loss. In humans, one PNPT1 allele class causes hearing loss with nothing else attached for decades, which is the strongest available statement that this tissue is selectively vulnerable rather than merely one of many.

evidence.snippet: We report here 2 siblings with PNPT1 mutations who presented delayed myelination as well as mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Reports delayed myelination as the presenting feature in a PNPT1 family.

steps/11.description: Two siblings with biallelic PNPT1 variants presented with delayed myelination rather than with a Leigh pattern, and delayed myelination was also seen in the patient with the p.Met485Val allele. White-matter change is common in the imaging series. Confidence is PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because the white matter is reached by two different routes in this disease - the bioenergetic one drawn here, and the interferon route that produces cystic leukoencephalopathy - and no study has separated their contributions in a single patient.

evidence.snippet: Longitudinal assessment of the interferon signature showed a massively elevated interferon score and chronic type I interferon-mediated autoinflammation.
evidence.explanation: Documents sustained interferon activation in a PNPT1 patient, measured over time rather than once.

steps/12.description:
Some patients with biallelic PNPT1 variants have a chronically elevated interferon signature in blood, and at least one presented as Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome with a massively elevated interferon score on longitudinal assessment. Two unrelated patients in a neuroimaging series had cystic leukoencephalopathy resembling RNASET2 deficiency, Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome or congenital CMV - imaging that is characteristic of an interferonopathy rather than of a respiratory-chain disorder.
This node is deliberately typed as a modifier and not as an obligatory step. The interferon response is documented in PNPT1 deficiency and plainly dominates some presentations; what has not been shown is how much it contributes to the encephalopathy of a typical COXPD13 patient. See the corresponding entry under discussions.

evidence.snippet: The patient also showed elevated lactate levels in the plasma.
evidence.explanation: Documents the raised plasma lactate in a genetically confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: blood and CSF lactate, and muscle respiratory chain enzyme assays were all normal
evidence.explanation: A genetically confirmed family in which lactate was normal. Recorded as REFUTE against any reading of this node as an obligatory finding; it does not refute the mechanism, only its universal expression.

steps/13.description: Lactate produced by glycolytic compensation raises plasma and sometimes CSF lactate. In this disease the elevation is a clue rather than a criterion: it is often only mild, and it was entirely normal in blood, CSF and muscle enzymology in one genetically confirmed family.

evidence.snippet: two siblings, born to consanguineous parents, with severe encephalomyopathy, choreoathetotic movements, and combined respiratory-chain defects
evidence.explanation: Reports choreoathetotic movements in the index patients.

steps/14.description: Choreoathetotic movements were the movement disorder in the founding siblings, and chorea has recurred in later patients. With dystonia it forms the hyperkinetic syndrome that, together with hypotonia and hearing loss, is the recognisable COXPD13 picture.

evidence.snippet: Currently, at 14 months, no neurodevelopment progress, dystonia, visual deficit, sensorineural deafness, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and microcephaly are observed.
evidence.explanation: Documents dystonia in a genetically confirmed infant.

steps/15.description: Dystonia is reported across the severity range, from the perinatal-onset patient to the adult siblings who developed it decades after congenital deafness.

evidence.snippet: a 34-month-old boy who presented with global developmental delay, muscular hypotonia, hearing impairment, and movement disorders including chorea and dystonia
evidence.explanation: Documents hearing impairment in a genetically confirmed patient with the full syndromic picture.

steps/16.description: Sensorineural hearing impairment is one of the disease's defining features and the one with the clearest tissue-level mechanism. It is not universal - it is inconstant in the most severe Leigh-like presentations - and it is also the sole feature of the allelic DFNB70 phenotype, which is curated separately.

evidence.snippet: two siblings, born to consanguineous parents, with severe encephalomyopathy, choreoathetotic movements, and combined respiratory-chain defects
evidence.explanation: Reports the severe encephalomyopathy in the index patients.

steps/17.description: Severe encephalomyopathy was the presentation of the index siblings and remains the core clinical statement of the disease. It is static in some patients and progressive in others; nothing published predicts which.

evidence.snippet: Two patients exhibited striatal lesions compatible with Leigh syndrome; one patient exhibited leukoencephalopathy and one patient had a normal brain MRI.
evidence.explanation: Reports the striatal Leigh-pattern lesion, and in the same sentence the imaging heterogeneity that keeps this from being a diagnostic criterion.

steps/18.description: The commonest neuroimaging finding, in a Leigh pattern - bilateral symmetrical signal change in the striatum and globus pallidus. It is not invariable: a neuroimaging series of six patients found striatal Leigh lesions in two, leukoencephalopathy in one, cystic leukoencephalopathy in two, and a normal MRI in one.

evidence.snippet: Our cases expand the phenotypic spectrum of PNPT1 mutations that can cause delayed myelination.
evidence.explanation: Establishes delayed myelination as part of the PNPT1 phenotypic spectrum.

steps/19.description: Delayed myelination was the presenting neuroimaging abnormality in two Japanese siblings and was also seen in the p.Met485Val patient, widening the imaging differential beyond the Leigh pattern.

evidence.snippet: one patient exhibited leukoencephalopathy and one patient had a normal brain MRI
evidence.explanation: Reports leukoencephalopathy among the imaging phenotypes of PNPT1 disease.

steps/20.description: White-matter disease, reported alongside the Leigh-pattern and normal-MRI phenotypes in the neuroimaging series.

evidence.snippet: We suggest that similar to RNASET2, PNPT1 be searched for in the setting of cystic leukoencephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: The authors' recommendation, which is the practical content of this phenotype.

steps/21.description: A cystic white-matter phenotype in two unrelated patients, indistinguishable on imaging from RNASET2 deficiency, Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome or congenital CMV infection. Curated as its own phenotype rather than folded into leukoencephalopathy because it is the imaging finding that argues for testing PNPT1 in a suspected interferonopathy. No HPO term distinguishes the cystic form, so the binding is the general leukoencephalopathy term and the specificity is carried by preferred_term.

evidence.snippet: Typically, it manifests during the neonatal period or infancy, presenting with severe encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and liver dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Lists lactic acidosis among the typical manifestations of COXPD13.

steps/22.description: Elevated lactate is a recurrent biochemical clue but a weak one - it is often only mildly raised, and it was normal in blood and CSF in one confirmed family.

evidence.snippet: characterized by feeding difficulties, dysphagia, muscle weakness, involuntary movements, muscle atrophy, abnormal eye movements, clouded vision, nystagmus, and decreased reflexes
evidence.explanation: Lists dysphagia among the features of the infantile decline, drawn from the reported COXPD13 case literature.

evidence.snippet: In instances where dystonia and dysphagia are observed during the neonatal period or infancy, and particularly when children experience unexplained mortality, it is advisable to conduct genetic testing promptly.
evidence.explanation: Gives dysphagia diagnostic rather than merely descriptive weight - paired with dystonia it is the authors' stated trigger for genetic testing.

steps/23.description: Difficulty swallowing, listed among the features of the sudden infantile decline that characterises this disease. It carries more weight than its position in a feature list suggests: the same review singles out dysphagia with dystonia in the neonatal or infantile period as the combination that should prompt prompt genetic testing, so it is a diagnostic trigger rather than only a burden. Mechanistically it sits with the bulbar dysfunction and brainstem signal change reported in PNPT1 disease.

evidence.snippet: characterized by feeding difficulties, dysphagia, muscle weakness, involuntary movements, muscle atrophy, abnormal eye movements, clouded vision, nystagmus, and decreased reflexes
evidence.explanation: Lists feeding difficulties among the features of the infantile decline, drawn from the reported COXPD13 case literature.

evidence.snippet: His feeding and sleeping patterns were poor, and he could not sit independently.
evidence.explanation: Documents poor feeding in the index Chinese patient at six months, the paper's own observation rather than its literature summary.

steps/24.description: Poor feeding is among the presenting signs of the infantile decline and, in the Chinese patient, poor feeding and sleeping were recorded at six months alongside the failure to achieve head control. It is the step between the swallowing problem and the growth failure, and it is what the feeding and nutritional arm of supportive care is directed at.

evidence.snippet: epilepsy, abnormalities in muscle tone and strength, global developmental delay, growth retardation, and visual and auditory impairment
evidence.explanation: Documents growth retardation in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/25.description: Growth failure with poor weight gain, marked enough in the Chinese patient to be diagnosed as severe malnutrition, and present as fetal growth restriction in the perinatal-onset patient. Feeding difficulty and dysphagia contribute, and are curated as their own phenotypes upstream of this one.

evidence.snippet: By 9 months, the patient experienced frequent convulsive seizures, displaying global hypotonia, significant muscle weakness, inability to control his head, and persistent bucofacial dyskinesias.
evidence.explanation: Records significant muscle weakness as an observation distinct from hypotonia in the index patient.

evidence.snippet: Increased muscle tone was noted in the back, with muscle strength rated at 3
evidence.explanation: The graded strength examination behind this phenotype. Quoted short because the full sentence's numeric range uses an en dash.

steps/26.description: Weakness is separable from the hypotonia it accompanies, and in the Chinese patient it was graded and asymmetric by segment - 3 to 4 out of 5 in the upper limbs but 0 in the lower limbs, with muscle atrophy and diminished lower-limb reflexes. The myopathic component is what the "myopathy" half of encephalomyopathy names.

edges/1.description: The missense substitutions act on the protein itself - on how the trimer assembles, how the S1 domains move, or on the active site.

evidence.snippet: the identified mutation results in a hypofunctional protein leading to disturbed PNPase trimerization and impaired mitochondrial RNA import
evidence.explanation: Directly connects the protein-level defect to the import defect in the same experimental series.

edges/2.description: PNPase is one of very few known components of the mammalian mitochondrial RNA-import machinery, and the hypofunctional protein imports less.

edges/3.description: In the matrix, PNPase is the ribonuclease half of the degradosome, so a crippled enzyme leaves transcripts unprocessed and degradation intermediates uncleared.

evidence.snippet: Finally, overexpression of the wild-type PNPT1 cDNA in fibroblasts of subject 1 induced an increase in 5S rRNA import in mitochondria and rescued the mitochondrial-translation deficiency.
evidence.explanation: A rescue experiment tying the two nodes together in the same cells - restoring import restored translation, which is what makes this an edge rather than a coincidence.

edges/4.description: The imported species feed mitochondrial gene expression - 5S rRNA has been proposed as a mitoribosomal component and RNase P RNA is needed for tRNA maturation - so under-supplying them limits translation.

edges/5.description: Transcripts that are never correctly matured cannot be translated, so the processing defect throttles mitochondrial protein synthesis independently of the import branch.

evidence.snippet: Loss of either enzyme results in massive accumulation of mitochondrial double-stranded RNA that escapes into the cytoplasm in a PNPase-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the causal step from degradosome loss to double-stranded RNA accumulation and escape.

edges/6.description: Bidirectional transcription of the mitochondrial genome generates complementary transcripts; the degradosome is what normally keeps the resulting duplexes from persisting.

edges/7.description: The thirteen mtDNA-encoded products are distributed across complexes I, III, IV and V, so under-supplying them makes those complexes fail together.

evidence.snippet: This process engages an MDA5-driven antiviral signalling pathway that triggers a type I interferon response.
evidence.explanation: Names the sensor and the pathway that carries this edge.

edges/9.description: Cytosolic double-stranded RNA is read by MDA5 as a viral signature.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, two unrelated patients exhibited cystic leukoencephalopathy resembling RNASET2-deficient patients, patients with Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) or congenital CMV infection.
evidence.explanation: Marked INDIRECT because the finding is a radiological resemblance across diseases sharing interferon activation, which supports the edge by analogy rather than by demonstrating the step.

edges/10.description: The intermediates are unknown. The association rests on imaging resembling other interferonopathies in two unrelated patients, not on a demonstrated interferon-to-white-matter mechanism in this disease.

edges/11.description: Glycolytic compensation converts accumulating pyruvate to lactate.

edges/15.description: Skeletal muscle is among the oxidative-demand tissues that fail, and the myopathic weakness is the "myopathy" of the encephalomyopathy this disease was first described as.

evidence.snippet: lower limbs spasticity and bulbar dysfunction were novel phenotypic findings
evidence.explanation: Reports the bulbar dysfunction named as this edge's intermediate, in the same patient whose imaging showed brainstem involvement. Marked INDIRECT because it establishes the intermediate rather than the swallowing outcome.

edges/21.description: Drawn as indirect with a named intermediate. Brainstem signal change and bulbar dysfunction are both reported in PNPT1 patients, and dysphagia is reported among the disease's features, but no source measures the swallow against the brainstem lesion in one patient - so the intermediate is stated rather than the edge asserted as direct.

edges/25.description: An unsafe or ineffective swallow is the proximate reason oral intake fails.

edges/26.description: Inadequate intake is the proximate cause of the poor weight gain, which in this patient reached the threshold of severe malnutrition.

evidence.snippet: PNPT1 is a mitochondrial RNA transport protein that has been linked to two discrete phenotypes, namely isolated sensorineural hearing loss (OMIM 614934) and combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency (OMIM 614932).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the two recessive PNPT1 entities and the OMIM numbers that separate them, which is what keeps DFNB70 out of this entry.

evidence.snippet: This study identifies PNPT1 as a new SCA gene, responsible for SCA25, and highlights biological links between alterations of mtRNA trafficking, interferonopathies and ataxia.
evidence.explanation: Documents the third, dominantly inherited PNPT1 entity, which is the reason zygosity and allele class have to be checked before a PNPT1 variant is read as COXPD13.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists for COXPD13 and no interventional trial has been run. Management is supportive - seizure control, nutritional and feeding support directed at the dysphagia and feeding difficulties curated as phenotypes here, developmental therapies, hearing and vision support, and surveillance - together with avoidance of the metabolic stressors that destabilise mitochondrial disease generally, such as prolonged fasting, dehydration, fever and untreated infection. That last part is extrapolated from mitochondrial medicine at large, not from evidence in this disease.

evidence.snippet: In patient treatment with adrenocorticotropic hormones proved ineffective, prompting the initiation of oral antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam and topiramate.
evidence.explanation: Reports the treatment given and one negative result. It supports the existence of this management step, not its efficacy - no outcome is given for the drugs that replaced the hormone.

treatments/1.description: Seizures and infantile spasms are treated conventionally. The one reported experience is discouraging and worth recording: adrenocorticotropic hormone was ineffective for infantile spasms in the Chinese patient, and levetiracetam and topiramate were started instead. That is a single patient, so it is a data point rather than guidance. Only the two drugs actually continued are listed as therapeutic agents; the hormone that failed is named here but deliberately kept out of that list, so the structured field is not read as a therapy this disease responds to.

evidence.snippet: In patient treatment with adrenocorticotropic hormones proved ineffective, prompting the initiation of oral antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam and topiramate.
evidence.explanation: Names the seizure phenotype these two drugs were started for. No outcome is reported for them, so this supports the targeting relationship and not efficacy.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Symptomatic seizure control. This targets a clinical manifestation rather than an upstream mechanism node, which is the honest placement - nothing in this disease's causal chain is treated by an antiseizure drug.

evidence.snippet: These results enabled the parents of these two boys to proceed to pregnancy planning using preimplantation genetic diagnosis
evidence.explanation: Documents the reproductive use to which a molecular diagnosis was put in a reported family.

treatments/2.description: Autosomal recessive inheritance gives a one-in-four recurrence risk per pregnancy for carrier couples. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis has been used successfully after a molecular diagnosis in this disease.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Both arms are demonstrated. Cytosolic mitochondrial double-stranded RNA and interferon-stimulated gene upregulation have been shown in PNPT1 patients themselves, one patient met criteria for Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, and two unrelated patients had interferonopathy-pattern cystic leukoencephalopathy. The respiratory-chain arm is equally well demonstrated.
What nobody has done is measure both in the same patients and relate them to which features those patients have. So it is not known whether the interferon response is a parallel disease mechanism, a modifier of severity, or a marker with little phenotypic consequence in patients whose presentation is encephalomyopathic rather than interferonopathic. This matters practically: if the interferon arm is causal in some patients, JAK inhibition - used in other interferonopathies - would be a rational thing to test, and nothing in the respiratory-chain model suggests any therapy at all. The entry types the interferon node as a modifier for now, which is the weakest claim consistent with the evidence.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The two founding 2012 papers framed the disease as an RNA-import defect, and measured reduced import of 5S rRNA, MRP RNA and RNase P RNA in patient fibroblasts, with rescue on re-expression. The 2017 Leigh-syndrome study reached the same disease by a different route: those alleles left the trimer intact, accumulated unprocessed ND6 transcripts, and the authors noted explicitly that the role and location of PNPase within human mitochondria remain contested.
The entry draws both branches because both are measured, and converges them on mitochondrial translation. But if one branch dominates, the other is carrying weight it has not earned, and no study has yet dissected an import-specific from a processing-specific allele in the same system. A separation-of-function allele series would settle it.

open_questions/2.rationale:
Complex V contains two mtDNA-encoded subunits, so a general mitochondrial translation defect predicts it should fall with complexes I, III and IV. In the one patient study that measured all five, it did not: complexes II and V were both unchanged while I, III and IV were reduced. Complex II sparing is expected and mechanistically explained; complex V sparing is not.
Only one family has been assayed this way, and the assay was steady-state subunit protein rather than enzyme activity, so this may be an artefact of method or of tissue. It is recorded because the standard summary of this disease class - complexes I, III, IV and V down with II spared - does not match the only complete measurement available in this gene, and a curator should not propagate the summary as if it had been observed here.

open_questions/3.rationale:
The clinical range is extreme - from a patient dead at 2.4 years to a 78-year-old survivor - and the study that assembled the whole reported cohort concluded that no genotype-phenotype correlation is established. The obvious hypothesis is that residual PNPase activity sets severity and that different structural defects preferentially disable different functions: the trimer-interface alleles, the conformation-restricting alleles and the active-site alleles could plausibly break import, processing and double-stranded RNA clearance in different proportions.
Nothing has tested this. No study has related a measured residual activity to a clinical outcome, and modifier genes have not been sought. Until that is done the entry cannot say why the same gene gives such different diseases, and the phenotype frequencies recorded here should be read as observations across a two-dozen-patient literature rather than as properties of the disease.

evidence.snippet: A major transport function of the human intestine involves the absorption of chloride in exchange for bicarbonate.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the physiological transport step whose loss defines this node.

evidence.snippet: By mRNA in situ hybridization, we demonstrate that the expression of DRA occurs preferentially in highly differentiated colonic epithelial cells, is unchanged in Finnish CLD patients with delta V317
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the cell type in which DRA acts and the point that transcript expression is preserved in the Finnish founder genotype, so the lesion is functional rather than transcriptional.

steps/0.description: The initiating lesion. DRA (SLC26A3) is a sodium-independent chloride/bicarbonate exchanger expressed at the apical membrane of differentiated ileal and colonic epithelium, where it performs the major chloride-absorbing step of the intestine, taking up luminal chloride in exchange for bicarbonate. Biallelic loss-of-function variants abolish or severely reduce this exchange. Notably, transcript expression can be preserved - the Finnish V317del allele is expressed at normal levels - so the lesion is loss of transport function at the apical membrane rather than loss of the gene product, which is what makes pharmacological rescue of residual protein conceivable.

evidence.snippet: It results from a reduced activity of the down regulated in adenoma exchanger (DRA), due to mutations in the solute carrier family 26, member 3 (SLC26A3) gene.
evidence.explanation: Links reduced DRA exchanger activity to the intestinal chloride malabsorption that defines this node.

evidence.snippet: The main feature of this condition is a severe chronic osmotic diarrhea that causes a secondary volume contraction
evidence.explanation: Describes the luminal osmotic consequence of the transport failure and the volume contraction it produces.

evidence.snippet: As early as the prenatal period, importantly, signs similar to those seen in the setting of intestinal obstruction, such as dilated intestinal loops on ultrasound, may be apparent.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that failure of intestinal fluid absorption begins in fetal life, producing dilated bowel loops that mimic obstruction - the reason affected neonates are sometimes taken to laparotomy before the diagnosis is made.

steps/1.description: The rate-limiting step. Chloride that cannot be absorbed accumulates in the ileal and colonic lumen as an osmotically active anion, obligating water retention and abolishing the net fluid absorption that normally occurs across the distal intestine. Because the failed step handles an ion rather than an ingested nutrient, luminal chloride load is set by secretion and diet-salt intake rather than by any single dietary constituent - which is why, unlike the diet-induced congenital diarrheas, the diarrhea cannot be abolished by eliminating a food. Fluid loss begins in fetal life, producing dilated fetal bowel loops and marked polyhydramnios.

evidence.snippet: severe chronic osmotic diarrhea that causes a secondary volume contraction with the development of metabolic alkalosis, electrolytes imbalance, failure to thrive, psycho-motor delay and even death
evidence.explanation: Names the full systemic consequence set of this node - metabolic alkalosis, electrolyte imbalance, failure to thrive, psychomotor delay and mortality - and attributes it to volume contraction from the diarrhea.

steps/2.description: The systemic arm, and the source of the disorder's diagnostic signature. Two processes combine. Stool loss of chloride, sodium and potassium depletes each ion, producing hypochloremia, hyponatremia and hypokalemia. Separately, DRA normally secretes bicarbonate into the lumen in exchange for the chloride it absorbs; when the exchanger fails, that bicarbonate is retained in the body. Retained bicarbonate plus chloride depletion plus volume-contraction-driven secondary hyperaldosteronism produce a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic ALKALOSIS. This is the mirror image of congenital sodium diarrhea, in which failure of sodium/proton exchange causes metabolic ACIDOSIS, and the acid-base direction is what distinguishes the two at the bedside.

evidence.snippet: The clinical presentation of CLD is a lifetime, potentially fatal diarrhoea with a high chloride content.
evidence.explanation: States the clinical output and the high stool chloride content that is the diagnostic hallmark of this node.

evidence.snippet: The quality of life in CLD patients is negatively influenced by the elevated number of evacuations a day and the fecal incontinence
evidence.explanation: Documents the residual disease burden that persists on salt substitution, supporting the distinction between correcting electrolytes and reducing stool volume.

steps/3.description: The clinical output. Lifelong profuse watery diarrhea whose stool chloride concentration exceeds the sum of stool sodium and potassium - the finding that clinches the diagnosis. Untreated, volume contraction and electrolyte depletion cause failure to thrive, psychomotor delay, renal impairment from chronic hypovolemia and hypokalemia, and death. Treated with salt substitution, electrolytes normalise and survival and growth are good, but stool volume remains high, so quality of life is dominated by the number of daily evacuations and by fecal incontinence.

evidence.snippet: we report segregation of two missense mutations, delta V317 and H124L, and one frameshift mutation, 344delT, of DRA in 32 Finnish and four Polish CLD patients
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery report identifying the causative DRA/SLC26A3 variants and their segregation in Finnish and Polish patients.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that DRA is an intestinal anion transport molecule that causes chloride diarrhoea when mutated.
evidence.explanation: States the causal conclusion linking the gene to the disease phenotype.

treatments/0.description: Lifelong oral sodium chloride and potassium chloride substitution is the life-saving mainstay of treatment. It replaces the ions lost in stool, restoring electrolyte balance and preventing metabolic alkalosis, and it transforms the prognosis of a disorder that is otherwise fatal. Its limitation is precise and important: it corrects the systemic consequences without acting on the intestinal transport defect, so stool volume is unchanged and the daily burden of diarrhea persists.

evidence.snippet: Oral salt substitutive therapy is a life-saving therapy: it improves the outcome, leads to electrolytes balance, reduces the risk of developing metabolic alkalosis, but has no effect on symptoms' severity
evidence.explanation: States exactly the scope and the limit of this treatment: life-saving and electrolyte-normalising, but without effect on diarrhea severity - which is why it is modelled as acting on the systemic node rather than the central effector.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replacing chloride, sodium and potassium orally offsets fecal losses and prevents the electrolyte depletion and alkalosis, acting on the systemic arm only and leaving the luminal transport defect untouched.

treatments/1.description: Oral sodium butyrate is the only therapy that reduces diarrhea severity itself. It acts by two routes: a DRA-independent route in which butyrate uptake stimulates the alternative anion exchanger PAT-1 and the sodium/proton exchangers NHE2 and NHE3 while inhibiting NKCC1, and a DRA-dependent route in which it increases SLC26A3 transcription and translation and reduces DRA mistrafficking and misfolding. Efficacy is genotype-dependent, best in patients with missense and deletion variants - consistent with rescue of residual protein - and some patients experience worsening at the standard 100 mg/kg/day dose. In those patients a step-up schedule from 50 mg/kg/day with weekly 25 mg/kg/day increments has restored responsiveness.

evidence.snippet: The effect of butyrate is related in part on a different modulation of the expression of the two main apical membrane Cl- exchangers of epithelial cells, members of the SLC26 anion family.
evidence.explanation: Attributes butyrate's effect to modulation of the two apical SLC26 chloride exchangers, supporting action on the trigger node.

evidence.snippet: The best response was observed in subjects with missense and deletion mutations.
evidence.explanation: Documents the genotype dependence of the response, consistent with rescue of residual mutant protein rather than replacement of an absent one.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Butyrate increases SLC26A3 expression and reduces DRA mistrafficking and misfolding, partially restoring the failed apical exchange step, and in parallel stimulates alternative chloride-absorbing transporters.

evidence.snippet: The step-up therapeutic approach resulted effective in limiting diarrhea severity in all our three previously unresponsive CLD patients.
evidence.explanation: Reports reduction in diarrhea severity with the step-up butyrate schedule in patients previously unresponsive to standard dosing.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Clinically, butyrate reduces diarrhea severity, the effect that distinguishes it from salt substitution.

evidence.snippet: D-Bifunctional protein deficiency (D-BPD) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by peroxisomal β-oxidation defects.
evidence.explanation: This identifies the peroxisomal beta-oxidation defect as the causal biochemical lesion.

evidence.snippet: HSD17B4 is essential in peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation, and mutations in HSD17B4 are associated in multiple autosomal recessive disorders, including D-bifunctional protein deficiency and Perrault syndrome.
evidence.explanation: This supports HSD17B4 as the causal gene for the peroxisomal beta-oxidation defect.

steps/1.description: Biallelic HSD17B4 pathogenic variants reduce peroxisomal D-bifunctional protein activity, disrupting the 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase and D-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase steps of peroxisomal beta-oxidation immediately downstream of the ACOX1 acyl-CoA oxidase step.

evidence.snippet: Very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) revealed significant increases in hexacosanoic acid (C26:0), tetracosanoic acid/docosanoic acid (C24:0/C22:0), and hexacosanoic acid/docosanoic acid (C26:0/C22:0).
evidence.explanation: This documents the characteristic VLCFA elevations in an affected patient.

evidence.snippet: The blood bile acid profile showed increased taurocholic acid, glycocholic acid, and taurochenodeoxycholic acid.
evidence.explanation: This supports accumulation of bile-acid species in affected patients.

steps/2.description: Impaired peroxisomal beta-oxidation causes accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids (C26:0 and abnormal ratios), branched-chain pristanic acid, and di-/trihydroxycholestanoic acid bile-acid intermediates.

evidence.snippet: However, progressive nystagmus, optic nerve atrophy, and bilateral hearing defects were observed and follow-up brain imaging revealed leukodystrophy and brain atrophy.
evidence.explanation: This documents leukodystrophy and brain atrophy on follow-up imaging.

evidence.snippet: Cranial MRI revealed bilateral hemispheric and callosal dysplasia, with schizencephaly in the right hemisphere.
evidence.explanation: This documents cortical/callosal malformation on neuroimaging in a severe neonatal case.

steps/3.description: Metabolite toxicity produces white-matter disease and progressive neurodegeneration affecting myelinating oligodendrocytes, with cortical malformation and brain atrophy in severe cases.

evidence.snippet: The typical symptoms include hypotonia and seizures.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports hypotonia as a typical feature.

steps/4.description: Hypotonia is a prominent early feature of DBP deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The typical symptoms include hypotonia and seizures.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports seizures as a typical feature.

steps/5.description: Intractable seizures are a typical neonatal feature.

evidence.snippet: follow-up brain imaging revealed leukodystrophy and brain atrophy
evidence.explanation: This supports leukodystrophy on neuroimaging.

steps/6.description: Progressive white-matter disease develops in affected infants.

evidence.snippet: neonatal hypotonia, seizures, craniofacial dysmorphisms, psychomotor delay, deafness, blindness
evidence.explanation: This lists psychomotor delay among the typical features.

steps/7.description: Affected children show profound psychomotor delay.

evidence.snippet: progressive nystagmus, optic nerve atrophy, and bilateral hearing defects were observed
evidence.explanation: This documents progressive hearing defects in an affected patient.

steps/8.description: Hearing impairment is part of the multisystem phenotype.

evidence.snippet: progressive nystagmus, optic nerve atrophy, and bilateral hearing defects were observed
evidence.explanation: This documents optic nerve atrophy in an affected patient.

steps/9.description: Optic nerve atrophy and visual loss occur in affected patients.

evidence.snippet: This patient showed craniofacial dysmorphism, club foot, and seizures with cyanosis one day after birth.
evidence.explanation: This documents craniofacial dysmorphism in an affected neonate.

steps/10.description: Zellweger-like craniofacial dysmorphism is characteristic of severe DBP deficiency.

evidence.snippet: D-bifunctional protein deficiency impairs the catabolism of very long chain fatty acids, DHCA and THCA, and pristanic acid resulting in accumulation of these metabolites.
evidence.explanation: This directly links the enzyme defect to accumulation of VLCFAs, bile-acid intermediates, and pristanic acid.

edges/1.description: Loss of DBP activity blocks peroxisomal oxidation of VLCFAs, pristanic acid, and bile-acid intermediates.

evidence.snippet: The deficiency of this peroxisomal enzyme leads to the accumulation of VLCFAs, causing multisystemic manifestations including the brain, retina, adrenal gland, hearing, and skeletal system.
evidence.explanation: This links substrate accumulation to multisystem (including CNS) disease.

edges/2.description: Accumulated VLCFAs and related metabolites are toxic to myelin and developing brain, driving leukodystrophy and progressive neurodegeneration.

edges/3.description: Severe peroxisomal beta-oxidation dysfunction in early development is associated with the Zellweger-like craniofacial dysmorphism seen in DBP deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Most common features are neonatal hypotonia for D-bifunctional protein deficiency and ovarian dysgenesis in females, sensorineural deafness, and other neurological abnormalities in Perrault syndrome
evidence.explanation: This documents the allelic relationship between DBP deficiency and Perrault syndrome at the HSD17B4 locus.

evidence.snippet: Supportive care is the main treatment, aiming at controlling symptoms
evidence.explanation: This supports supportive, symptom-directed care as the mainstay of management.

treatments/0.description: Management is supportive and symptom-directed, including antiepileptic therapy, feeding and respiratory support, and surveillance for sensory and neurologic decline. No disease-modifying therapy is established.

evidence.snippet: The patient had type III DBP deficiency; therefore, docosahexaenoic acid and non-soluble vitamins were administered.
evidence.explanation: This documents DHA and vitamin supplementation in an affected patient.

evidence.snippet: advocate for the early management of fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies to reduce complications
evidence.explanation: This supports early fat-soluble vitamin management.

treatments/1.description: Docosahexaenoic acid and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation has been used; early management of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency is advocated to reduce complications.

evidence.snippet: At 6 months of age, she had her first seizure, followed by frequent episodes of both febrile and non-febrile seizures, some requiring hospitalization.
evidence.explanation: Establishes fever as a recurrent seizure precipitant from disease onset in a reported patient.

evidence.snippet: At age 7 months she was admitted in status epilepticus with a febrile illness.
evidence.explanation: A second patient in whom a febrile illness precipitated status epilepticus.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to wild type human ARV1, neither variant expressed detectable levels of protein in mammalian cells.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates loss of ARV1 protein for the disease-associated variants, grounding the loss-of-function trigger.

evidence.snippet: The human ARV1 encodes a ubiquitously expressed 271-amino-acid protein containing the N-terminal ARV1 homology domain (AHD), which also includes a putative zinc-binding motif and the first of six predicted transmembrane domains
evidence.explanation: Source for the protein architecture (length, AHD, zinc-binding motif, transmembrane topology) described in this node.

steps/2.description: ARV1 is a ubiquitously expressed ~271-residue multi-pass ER transmembrane protein with an N-terminal conserved ARV1 homology domain carrying a putative zinc-binding motif. Biallelic variants reduce or abolish functional ARV1: truncating and frameshift alleles trigger nonsense-mediated decay, splice variants reduce transcript and protein and delete conserved domains, and missense/in-frame-deletion alleles fail (or only partially rescue) the temperature-sensitive growth defect of arv1-null yeast. Neither the p.Lys59_Asn98del nor the previously reported p.Gly189Arg allele produced detectable protein in mammalian cells.

evidence.snippet: ARV1 associates with PIGQ, a GPI-GnT component, and ARV1 mutants defective in this association lose their ability to enhance GPI-GnT activity, showing that association with PIGQ is critical for ARV1's function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the molecular mechanism by which ARV1 supports GPI-GnT activity and how its loss impairs the pathway.

evidence.snippet: complementation tests in yeast showed that the ARV1 p.Gly189Arg mutation leads to deficient maturation of Gas1, a GPI-anchored protein, but does not affect sphingolipid synthesis
evidence.explanation: Isolates the GPI-anchoring defect from the sphingolipid role for a patient allele, supporting GPI biosynthesis as the decisive lesion.

steps/3.description: The disease-relevant consequence of ARV1 loss is impaired initiation of GPI anchor biosynthesis. ARV1 associates with PIGQ within the GPI-GnT complex and promotes efficient recruitment of the phosphatidylinositol substrate; an ARV1 mutant unable to associate with PIGQ loses the ability to enhance GPI-GnT activity. In a complementation assay the human p.Gly189Arg allele caused deficient maturation of the GPI-anchored protein Gas1 without affecting sphingolipid synthesis, isolating the GPI-anchoring defect as the mechanistically decisive lesion. Whether ARV1's ancestral sterol/sphingolipid trafficking role contributes independently to neuronal injury is unresolved (see gap_gpi_versus_lipid_driver).

evidence.snippet: The splice variants resulted in decreased ARV1 expression and significant decreases in GPI-anchored protein on the membranes of neutrophils and fibroblasts, indicating that the loss of ARV1 results in impaired GPI-anchor synthesis.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of reduced surface GPI-anchored proteins in patient cells.
